review_notes: I read the whole file and the downstream `DegreeRigidity/Syntax` files that use it. There are no loops or competing rules among the @[simp] lemmas here: cons_zero, cons_succ, eval_disj, eval_allMem, eval_singleton, eval_unorderedPair, eval_orderedPair and eval_pairMem are all oriented toward a normal form of set-theoretic statements. I also checked that Formula.absolute is rightly not @[simp], because it needs hypotheses and would rewrite in the wrong direction. The only weakness I found is that `Formula.Eval` has no simp equations for its five constructors, so every client must name `Formula.Eval` in its simp set. I could not run Lean, so I have not tested the proposed change. If the annotation is added, some `simp only [...]` calls that list `Formula.Eval` might not need it, and clients that call plain `simp` on Eval of a concrete constructor could behave differently.

findings.excerpt:
| .conj φ ψ => Eval env φ ∧ Eval env ψ
  | .neg φ => ¬ Eval env φ
  | .existsMem i φ => ∃ x ∈ env i, Eval (cons x env) φ
findings.problem: The file builds a simp interface around `Formula.Eval`, but the semantic function has no simp equations of its own for `.equal`, `.member`, `.conj`, `.neg` or `.existsMem`. `eval_disj`, `eval_allMem`, `eval_singleton`, `eval_unorderedPair`, `eval_orderedPair` and `eval_pairMem` are all @[simp], so plain `simp` can use them on defined connectives. But `simp` cannot unfold `Eval` on the primitive constructors, so the derived-form lemmas only fire once the caller adds `Formula.Eval` by hand. The result is that nearly every client proof repeats `simp only [Formula.Eval, Formula.eval_..., cons_zero, cons_succ]` or `simp [Formula.Eval, ...]`. Examples are stepFormula, certificateFormula, graphFormula, rankFormula, allDomainMatrix and the SequenceTrace definability proofs. Several of these also list lemmas that are already @[simp], such as `Formula.eval_pairMem`.
findings.proposed_change: Make the constructor equations part of the default simp set. Either put `attribute [simp] Formula.Eval` after the definition, or state `eval_equal`, `eval_member`, `eval_conj`, `eval_neg` and `eval_existsMem` as @[simp] theorems proved by `Iff.rfl`. The `existsMem` one would read `(existsMem i φ).Eval env ↔ ∃ x ∈ env i, φ.Eval (cons x env)`. The rules cannot loop: they rewrite `Eval` on a constructor into `Eval` on strictly smaller subformulas. They also do not overlap the existing derived-form lemmas, which are about `disj`, `allMem`, `singleton` and the other defined formulas, not constructors. Leave `Realize` and `absolute` unannotated, since `absolute` needs hypotheses.
findings.benefit: Concrete formulas built from `.conj`, `.neg`, `.existsMem`, `.member` and `.equal` become evaluable by plain `simp`, and the existing @[simp] lemmas `eval_disj`, `eval_allMem`, `eval_pairMem` and `eval_orderedPair` then work automatically on them. Callers no longer need to know that `Formula.Eval` must be listed beside the library's own simp lemmas, and the long `simp only` lists in the downstream term and certificate proofs get shorter.
